---
title: "A structure puzzle: one formula, several kinds of evidence"
---

Allow 60 minutes for structure work and 45 minutes for the R plot. All spectra
and peak tables supplied here are **simulated teaching examples**, not measured
spectra. Values are illustrative, and simple splitting uses a first-order model.

## 1. Use the formula before looking at a spectrum

Unknown U1 has formula C₄H₈O₂. For this ordinary closed-shell C/H/O molecule,
the degree of unsaturation is `(2*C + 2 - H)/2`. Calculate it. Draw ethyl
ethanoate and butanoic acid, showing that both satisfy the formula.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked check"}
The degree is (8 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1. A carbonyl supplies one double bond in either
candidate. The formula alone does not decide whether the oxygens are arranged
as an ester or a carboxylic acid; it also does not rule out every other possible
connectivity. These are two candidate structures to test.
:::

## 2. Read the supplied evidence

U1 has strong IR absorption in the ester carbonyl region near 1740 cm⁻¹ and
no evident broad acid/alcohol O–H band in the supplied complete trace. Its
proton NMR peaks are:

| Shift / ppm | Multiplicity | Integral |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1.25 | triplet | 3H |
| 2.05 | singlet | 3H |
| 4.12 | quartet | 2H |

The proton-decoupled carbon NMR shows four signals at approximately 14, 21,
60 and 171 ppm. Assign every supplied observation to ethyl ethanoate. Explain
the quartet/triplet relationship and the acetyl methyl singlet.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
First find an O–CH₂–CH₃ fragment. The CH₂ sees three equivalent neighbouring
H; the CH₃ sees two. Then account for the remaining three protons.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked assignment"}
For CH₃COOCH₂CH₃: terminal ethyl CH₃ gives 1.25 ppm, triplet, 3H; O–CH₂ gives
4.12 ppm, quartet, 2H; acetyl CH₃ gives 2.05 ppm, singlet, 3H because the
adjacent carbonyl carbon has no H. The carbon signals correspond respectively
to terminal ethyl CH₃ (14), acetyl CH₃ (21), O–CH₂ (60) and C=O (171). Strong
carbonyl IR and no broad O–H agree with the ester. Peak heights in a schematic
NMR drawing are not the integrals; use the supplied areas/integral values.
:::

## 3. Try to reject the alternative

Explain two independent disagreements between butanoic acid and U1. What
would make an argument from an absent IR feature less reliable? Why is the
name of a supplied data file not evidence for chemical identity?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked reasoning"}
Butanoic acid would have an acid O–H region and no O–CH₂ quartet. It also
would not give the isolated acetyl methyl singlet of the ester. Absence is less
informative if the relevant region was not measured, the sample is too dilute,
or the signal is obscured. A filename is a label supplied by a person and can
be wrong; identity should be tested against the observations.
:::

## 4. R task: present an IR comparison

Open the [student project](../reference/data.qmd). The supplied `data/ir.csv`
contains `sample_id`, `wavenumber_cm1` and `transmittance_percent`. Plot the
simulated ethyl ethanoate and ethanoic acid traces. Keep their sample labels
so the plotted evidence can be traced back to the data.

```r
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
ir <- read_csv("data/ir.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
comparison <- ir |>
  filter(sample_id %in% c("ethyl_ethanoate", "ethanoic_acid"))
ggplot(comparison,
       aes(wavenumber_cm1, transmittance_percent, colour = sample_id)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  labs(x = "Wavenumber (cm−1)", y = "Transmittance (%)",
       colour = "Simulated sample") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Add a report caption explaining that these are simulated traces, that dips
indicate absorption in a transmittance plot, and which region distinguishes
the candidates. Use a descending wavenumber axis; it is conventional here and
does not reverse the underlying physics. Check that transmittance values lie
between 0 and 100. Do not fit a model or ask R to assign the unknown for you.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Interpretation check"}
The acid trace includes a very broad O–H region, while the ester trace lacks
that broad feature. Both contain carbonyl absorption. The chemical comparison
uses the functional groups expected from the candidate structures; the plot
is a way to inspect and communicate the supplied observations. An exact
carbonyl position is not a unique molecular fingerprint.
:::

## Leave with

A fully annotated structure, a rejected alternative, and a knitted Rmd section
with a labelled IR comparison. Read selected Solomons chapters 2 and 9 through
the [reading guide](../reference/reading.qmd).
